title: The Disney protests were a wake-up call about the risks of streaming mergers
gist: Using her own failed attempt to boycott Disney after the 2025 Kimmel suspension, Ars Technica's Scharon Harding argues that streaming M&A (Disney-Fubo, the proposed WBD-Skydance Paramount deal, Fox-Roku) is concentrating ownership, which tends to raise prices and makes consumer protest less effective. She points to licensing, cross-category bundles and better content discovery as alternative ways for streamers to grow revenue.

insights.claim: Boycotting Disney in 2025 over the Kimmel suspension meant giving up Disney+, Hulu, ABC, FX, ESPN, film franchises such as Avatar, Alien and Die Hard, some video games, and theme parks, because media consolidation has made Disney so far-reaching.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Owning a broad portfolio makes a conglomerate's revenue harder to boycott, which lowers its reputational downside risk.

insights.claim: The author reports that the Disney boycott did hit the company financially and pushed it to bring Jimmy Kimmel Live! back on air.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Coordinated subscriber cancellations can still move a conglomerate's behavior, so they are a real headline risk for media stocks.
insights.quote: It has been reported that the boycott financially impacted Disney and put pressure on the company to get Kimmel back on.

insights.claim: The author argues that as streaming ownership shrinks to fewer companies, consumers find it harder to cut ties with a provider they object to, and smaller voices find it harder to be heard.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Concentration gives streamers pricing power and reduces churn after controversies.

insights.claim: Disney sold its stakes in A&E, History and Lifetime to Hearst.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Disney is shedding non-core cable network stakes.
insights.quote: Disney has since sold its stake in those networks to Hearst

insights.claim: In February 2024 Fubo sued Disney, Fox and Warner Bros. Discovery on antitrust grounds over their planned joint sports streaming app, alleging that Disney forced it to pay millions a year for non-sports content it did not want in order to get sports rights.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Forced bundling of sports rights is the main source of leverage incumbents hold over virtual MVPDs.
insights.locator: Disney settled an antitrust lawsuit through acquisition

insights.claim: In January 2025 Disney made Fubo's antitrust suit go away by acquiring Fubo, after which Fubo said it no longer objected to the Disney/Fox/WBD sports app. That app was canceled anyway.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Incumbents can use M&A to buy out antitrust challengers, a playbook regulators may start scrutinizing.
insights.quote: In January 2025, Disney effectively made the antitrust suit go away by buying Fubo.

insights.claim: Fubo's complaint said Disney and Fox held monopoly power in the sports programming market.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: These monopoly allegations are on the record and could resurface in future merger reviews.
insights.quote: had “monopoly power in the sports programming market.”
insights.locator: Disney settled an antitrust lawsuit through acquisition

insights.claim: In July Fubo raised monthly prices by $15 after a carriage dispute with NBCUniversal. Once the dispute was settled, it charged more than before while carrying fewer NBCU channels.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Programmers are winning carriage fights and the cost increases are being passed to subscribers, which supports content-owner pricing power.

insights.claim: Fubo's higher price also covers non-sports channels it was required to restore, including Brazo, Cozi and True CRMZ, which suggests bundling obligations are inflating costs at a sports-focused service.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Forced bundling squeezes vMVPD margins and pushes up consumer prices.

insights.claim: Experts the author has interviewed consistently expect more streaming mergers, because services launched at unsustainably low prices to grow subscribers now face pressure to become profitable.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Expect continued deal flow and consolidation premia among subscale streamers.
insights.quote: Streaming services launched at unsustainably low prices aimed at growing subscriptions.

insights.claim: Mergers let streaming companies manage content costs and build larger libraries that draw more subscribers and advertisers.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Scale in content libraries is the main strategic reason for streaming M&A.

insights.claim: A combined WBD and Skydance Paramount would put HBO Max, Discovery+, CNN, Paramount+, CBS and Pluto TV under one owner.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: This would be a major consolidation of premium and FAST streaming assets, with a large regulatory and political overhang.

insights.claim: The author argues that merging streaming services could reduce content fragmentation but would likely raise subscription prices, because of higher content costs, bigger libraries and less competition.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Consolidation should support ARPU growth at the expense of consumer surplus.

insights.claim: Fox's planned purchase of Roku would put two FAST services, Tubi and The Roku Channel, under one owner, which could reduce free streaming choice and extend Fox's approach to ad loads and conservative programming to The Roku Channel.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Fox-Roku would concentrate the FAST market and could draw antitrust scrutiny.

insights.claim: Licensing content to other platforms more often could earn streamers extra revenue and ease fragmentation, although niche services risk diluting the exclusives that set them apart.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Content licensing is a revenue lever that does not require M&A, but it comes with a cost to differentiation.

insights.claim: Discounts for linking a streaming subscription to home internet or mobile service reportedly reduce cancellations, and bundles with music, gaming or food delivery could reach younger viewers.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Telcos and delivery platforms gain value as distribution partners because they reduce streamer churn.

insights.claim: Deloitte argues that media companies' current bundles may miss the mark because younger subscribers want broader cross-category ecosystems.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Cross-category bundle partnerships are where growth may lie.
insights.quote: younger subscribers look toward broader cross-category ecosystems

insights.claim: In Gracenote's 2025 State of Play survey of 3,000 consumers in six countries, 49 percent said they would cancel a service because it was hard to find something to watch.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Content discovery, including AI-driven recommendation, is directly tied to churn.

insights.claim: Some streaming services already use generative AI chatbots for content discovery, but reliable discovery that people enjoy remains an unsolved problem across streamers, smart TV OS owners, marketers and AI companies.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: There is an opening for AI recommendation vendors and TV OS platforms.
